newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Sugar-Far East market slow, waits on China.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar-Far East market slow, waits on China.

text.p: The Far Eastern sugar market has been lulled, like the region, into holiday doldrums, with some traders hoping Chinese sugar producers will liven things up with exports, industry and trade sources said on Wednesday.
Prices for Chinese sugar in the major producing region of Guangxi have not moved above 3,800 yuan ($457) a tonne for two months, a China Sugar Association official told Reuters.
Tokyo traders said they were keeping a close watch on China's domestic sugar prices, which they saw as a key to when the country will enter the world market.
Chinese wholesale prices for white sugar had been expected to firm in the lead-up to the Lunar New Year holiday, China's premier annual festival when demand for confectionary traditionally soars.
This year was an exception, regional traders just returned from their five-day break said, and now they were waiting for the end of the Chinese crushing season in late March.
The sugar association representative, who spoke anonymously from Guangxi, said it was impossible to know if and when prices would firm because domestic demand remains flat.
One trader with a Western bank suggested China could take advantage of healthy Asian premiums to earn $15 to $20 a tonne on white sugar exports.
With Indonesia buying Thai whites, the way could be left open for increased demand for Chinese white sugar, possibly from Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and the Philippines, the Western trading source said.
The current premium, on a white to raw basis, is around $70 a tonne, traders said.
But the freight advantage of Far Eastern whites adds another $20 a tonne, bringing the premium up to $90 a tonne, the Western trader said.
"What you could find is that existing (Chinese) stocks could be put up for export," he said. "You could find that people would get a better return by exporting."
The China Sugar Association representative said he doubted Chinese sugar would hit the regional market, as prices were still too low for the government to justify granting licences.
He said Gaungxi, which produces most of China's cane sugar, has 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes of processed sugar in reserve.
The central government had agreed to buy locally produced stock to shore up prices, he said.
This made the notion of exports unlikely in the near term, he said.
If and when the ex-factory price for white sugar moves above 4,400 yuan per tonne, these stocks would be released on to the market, a Hong Kong trader said.
Nor were imports, which the government has said will hit 690,000 tonnes in 1997, seen happening any time before prices begin to firm, he said.
Traders in Tokyo said they expected Thai raw sugar premiums to remain weak this week, because of the lull in physical buying in the Far East.
Thai premiums for March/May delivery were quoted at 0.20/0.25 cents (bid/offer) per pound over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on an FOB (free on board) basis.
May/July deliveries were quoted at about 0.30 cents on the New York exchange, they said.
One of few movements in physical trading was Wednesday's retender by state-owned Taiwan Sugar Corp, traders said.
On January 31, it passed on a tender in New York for a 30,000-tonne shipment. The shipment was slated for April delivery.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-7004
-- Eiichiro Tokumoto, Tokyo Commodities Desk (81-3) 3432-7391
